title: Global consumers are switching between premium and value modes as trust and perceived payoff determine what earns a place in the basket
source_unit: NIQ and World Data Lab, A Tale of Two Consumers: The polarized mindsets reshaping global consumption
geography: Global FMCG markets with consumer-class, generational, regional, and United States comparisons

observations.period: 2021-2025; global fast-moving consumer-goods prices and household basket pressure

denominator.unit: markets in the report's latest price comparison, with broader historical comparison across NIQ market data

fmcg_price_increase.unit: percent increase in global FMCG prices from 2021 through 2025

consumer_response.value: Households became more deliberate about which products deserve more money, what should cost less, and what leaves the basket

confidence_spending_gap.value: Consumer confidence is described as historically weak while aggregate spending continues to grow, with growth unevenly distributed

basket_meaning.value: Inflation is converting macroeconomic pressure into category- and occasion-level decisions about trust, utility, identity, and perceived payoff

observations.method: NIQ synthesis of survey, consumption, shopper, and price-tier data combined with World Data Lab income, spending, and demographic projections.
observations.uncertainty: The report combines commercial data, survey measures, and projections with different denominators and markets; price changes and aggregate spending do not establish household welfare, real income, or causal purchase responses.
observations.subgroup: FMCG shoppers across income groups, generations, markets, categories, channels, and price tiers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater selectivity can reflect consumer agency and improved comparison as well as financial stress; aggregate spending growth can conceal both affordability loss and category substitution.

observations.period: 2026; global consumer classes and concentration of spending

denominator.unit: global population frame used by World Data Lab and NIQ

core_consumers.unit: core consumers spending approximately $13–$90 per person per day

affluent_consumers.unit: affluent consumers spending more than $90 per person per day

per_capita_spending.value: Annual per-capita spending is projected at approximately $54,700 for affluent consumers versus $7,900 for core consumers

2026_spending.value: Affluent consumers are projected to account for $35.9 trillion of 2026 spending versus $31.6 trillion for core consumers despite being far fewer in number
2026_spending.unit: nominal U.S. dollars, projected global spending

observations.method: World Data Lab consumer-class definitions and income, spending, and demographic projections summarized by NIQ.
observations.uncertainty: These are modeled consumer classes and nominal spending projections, not household survey counts of realized purchasing power, disposable income, or equal access to goods; class thresholds and currency assumptions matter.
observations.subgroup: Affluent and core consumer classes across mature and emerging markets, with different population growth, income mobility, and category access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large aggregate spending by affluent consumers does not mean every affluent household is unconstrained, while core-market expansion can create meaningful improvements in access even when per-capita spending remains lower.

observations.period: 2026; upgrade and price-constrained consumer mindsets across categories and generations

denominator.unit: consumer-mindset framework spanning generations, income levels, markets, categories, and occasions

behavioral_divide.value: Upgrade and price-constrained modes appear across every income level and generation and shift by category, need state, occasion, region, and perceived value

upgrade_value.unit: percent of upgrade consumers focusing on value for money

upgrade_convenience.unit: percent of upgrade consumers willing to pay for convenience

lower_price_switching.value: One-third of price-constrained consumers switch to lower-priced options or buy whichever brand is on promotion

selective_premium.value: Price-constrained consumers may still trade up when quality, health, transparency, utility, identity, or convenience makes the payoff defensible

observations.method: NIQ consumer and shopper research organized into a commercial upgrade/value framework, with price-tier and category examples.
observations.uncertainty: The framework is designed for market strategy and does not provide a representative causal model of household decision-making; self-reported attitudes may not match observed purchases, especially across markets.
observations.subgroup: Upgrade-oriented and price-constrained shoppers, private-label buyers, brand buyers, generations, and households facing different time, care, health, and budget pressures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Selective premiumization can be a form of constrained optimization rather than prosperity; promotion-driven switching does not necessarily imply weak brand trust if private label is perceived as equivalent or superior.

denominator.unit: global regional and market projection frame

western_core_share.value: North America and Europe's share of the global core-consumer population is projected to fall from 41% to 13% by 2036

emerging_market_runway.value: Africa, emerging Asia, and Latin America are described as adding mass-market volume through population growth, income mobility, and category development

us_barbell.value: In the United States, premium growth and value-seeking are expanding at opposite ends while mainstream categories are pressured, with premium private label contributing to some category growth

geographic_meaning.value: Global consumer culture is diverging by both purchasing power and the local route through which households gain access to premium, value, convenience, and culturally relevant products

observations.method: NIQ market and category analysis combined with World Data Lab regional income, population, and consumer-class projections.
observations.uncertainty: The 2036 figures are projections, not forecasts guaranteed to materialize; market-level growth does not establish household inclusion, local producer gains, or culturally equivalent consumption across regions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. and mature-market households, emerging-market consumers, private-label and national-brand shoppers, retailers, and local producers.
observations.counterinterpretation: A shrinking Western share of core consumers can coexist with high absolute purchasing power and new premium markets; U.S. middle-market pressure varies by department and does not imply uniform household behavior.

observations.period: 2026; AI, social commerce, and discovery-led purchase pathways

denominator.unit: NIQ global consumer-discovery report frame; exact shopper sample and country bases are not disclosed in the press release

ai_product_discovery.unit: percent of shoppers reported as using AI during product discovery

western_social_discovery_purchase.value: nearly one-third of Western consumers have purchased a product after discovering it on a social platform

apac_social_quick_commerce.value: nearly 60% of APAC consumers shop through social and quick-commerce channels

retail_media_market.unit: billion U.S. dollars in reported global retail-media market size

discovery_conversion_route.value: AI, retail media, and social commerce move influence earlier in the purchase journey, from discovery and evaluation toward transaction

observations.method: NIQ and World Data Lab press-release summary of global consumer, retail-media, and social-commerce research; the release does not disclose the underlying shopper sample, questionnaire, weighting, or transaction linkage.
observations.uncertainty: The reported percentages are commercial research toplines and the retail-media figure is a market estimate; discovery or reported purchase does not establish conversion rate, product quality, consumer welfare, platform causality, or durable channel substitution.
observations.subgroup: Global shoppers, Western consumers, APAC consumers, AI users, social-commerce users, brands, retailers, creators, and retail-media intermediaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI use may be exploratory and social discovery may coexist with stores, search, friends, and retailer channels; market growth can reflect advertising reclassification or platform monetization rather than better consumer choice.

boundary: This record adds a global consumer-culture route from inflation and unequal spending power through situational premiumization, trade-down, trust, identity, convenience, private label, generational influence, and regional divergence. It is a commercial publisher synthesis combining surveys, shopper and market data, and modeled projections; it is not a probability household panel, causal welfare analysis, or proof that reported value perceptions produce realized health, cultural, or financial outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official NIQ report page was reviewed for global FMCG price change, consumer classes, spending projections, upgrade and price-constrained mindsets, trust/value triggers, regional projections, and U.S. category patterns.
